headline: Three wild dogs trekked 2,500 miles to find a mate
summary: Three African wild dog brothers zigzagged across Zambia for eight months, covering 2,485 miles, the longest recorded trip by any African land mammal looking for a mate. They skirted the capital, Lusaka, and other built-up areas. Three sisters set out on a similar trek, but two died in illegal snares. Only about 6,000 wild dogs are left.

cover_question.q: Why did they walk so far?

cover_answer: To find a mate. They can't pair up in their own pack.
table_question: How far would you go to find your people?

5-7.script: Three wild dog brothers in Africa walked for eight months looking for a new family. They went 2,500 miles, farther than driving from Chicago to Los Angeles. They went around the big cities. They made it, and the scientists who tracked them are hopeful.
5-7.why: Three brothers on a long walk is a story a five-year-old can hold. The distance is the wow.

8-12.script: Wild dogs can't have pups in their own pack, so at two or three they leave to find a mate. Three brothers walked 2,485 miles across Zambia, zigzagging around cities like a road trip with every highway closed. Two of three sisters died in snares.
8-12.why: The leaving rule is the mechanism. Kids get why you'd go.

13-17.script: If wild animals need a path through farms and towns, who gives up the land? Three wild dog brothers crossed 2,485 miles of Zambia to find a mate and made it. Two of three sisters on the same trip died in snares. Half empty or half full?
13-17.why: Teens like a real trade-off. The scientist's line hands them one.

5-7.a: The story doesn't say. What it says is they made the whole trip safely, and that's the hard part.

8-12.q: Why did they walk so far?
8-12.a: Wild dogs can't have pups in the pack they're born in, so they leave to find a mate. These three went 2,485 miles because cities and farms were in the way.
A wire loop poachers hide on the ground to catch animals. It's illegal. Two of the three sisters on the same kind of trip died in them.

13-17.q: Why does it matter if only 6,000 are left?
13-17.a: That's the point. If packs can still reach each other, they can mix and survive. The study says every big population may still be connected.

13-17.q: Isn't it grim that the sisters died?
13-17.a: It is. The lead scientist called it half empty and half full. The fix he wants is strips of wild land linking the parks.
